title: When the Patient Says No

patient.name: Mdm Lim Bee Geok
patient.presenting_complaint: Annual diabetic eye review — scheduled for dilated fundus examination

history.hpc: Mdm Lim is a 64-year-old with Type 2 diabetes for 12 years, attending for her annual dilated fundus exam. When the OA explains that eye drops are needed to dilate her pupils, Mdm Lim becomes visibly anxious and says: 'No, I don't want those drops. My neighbour went blind after getting eye drops at another clinic. I'm not doing it.' She is cooperative otherwise but firm in her refusal. She has had dilation before at her previous clinic 2 years ago with no problems, though she does not seem to recall this clearly.
history.pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 12 years (HbA1c 8.2% last check). Hypertension. No known drug allergies. Previous uneventful dilated fundus exam 2 years ago.
history.allergies: No drug allergy recorded on file.
history.social_hx: Retired. Came alone today. Does not drive. Plans to take MRT home.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Clear cornea. Pupils normally reactive. No contraindications to dilation identified on external assessment.
examination_findings.fundus: Cannot be assessed without dilation — this is why dilation is clinically indicated

investigations.va_distance: Measured with habitual correction. RE: LogMAR 0.2. LE: LogMAR 0.3.
investigations.iop_nct: RE: 17 mmHg. LE: 16 mmHg. Measured prior to any drops.

diagnosis: Patient refuses dilation despite clinical indication (diabetic eye screening). Refusal is based on misinformation about a neighbour's outcome. The OA must address concerns, provide correct information, and escalate to the doctor if refusal persists. If refusal is maintained after proper counselling, it must be documented and the doctor informed.

immediate: Stay calm, do not argue or dismiss the patient's concerns
Acknowledge her fear: 'I understand you are worried, Mdm Lim. Can you tell me more about what happened to your neighbour?'
Clarify the misunderstanding: dilating drops do not cause blindness — her neighbour's problem was almost certainly unrelated to the drops

Explain why dilation is needed specifically for her: 'You have diabetes for 12 years. Diabetes can affect the blood vessels at the back of your eye silently — no pain, no symptoms until it is very late. The only way to see this is to dilate your pupils and look inside.'
Explain the drops used: tropicamide — approved eye drops, used millions of times worldwide, temporary blurring for 4-6 hours, then vision returns to normal
Remind her she had dilation before without problems (if she recalls)
If she still refuses after counselling: DO NOT instil drops — you cannot force a patient
Inform the doctor immediately about the refusal and the reason
Document the refusal in the patient's record: date, time, reason given, education provided, outcome
follow_up: Doctor to speak with patient — may be able to address concerns further
If patient still refuses after speaking with doctor, arrange a follow-up appointment
Refusal must be documented as an informed refusal with the doctor's signature
Schedule a follow-up date — diabetic eye disease can progress, so patient should return soon
patient_education: Dilating drops do not cause blindness — vision blurring is temporary (4-6 hours)
Diabetic eye disease is silent — the examination is essential to detect it before vision is lost
Not checking the back of the eye is actually the greater risk for someone with her history
She can bring a family member next time if she would feel more comfortable

key_points: Listens to the patient's concern without dismissing or arguing
Elicits the specific reason for refusal (neighbour anecdote / fear of blindness)
Notes the patient's diabetes duration and clinical risk (12 years, HbA1c elevated)
Recalls or checks that the patient has had dilation before without incident
Acknowledges the fear with empathy before providing information
Completes measurements that can be done without drops (VA and IOP) — does not delay these
Does NOT instil any drops without consent
Accurately documents all findings including the refusal event in the correct format
Checks for any allergy or contraindication proactively while explaining the drops
Correctly identifies this as an informed refusal situation — not a non-compliant patient
Understands the clinical stakes: diabetic retinopathy can be missed without dilation
Recognises that patient autonomy must be respected if refusal persists after full counselling
Escalates to the doctor appropriately — does not handle the final decision alone
Does not force or coerce the patient — respects autonomy
Provides accurate, non-alarming information that directly addresses the patient's fear
Escalates to doctor when refusal persists after initial counselling
Documents the refusal with full details including counselling provided and doctor informed
Arranges follow-up to ensure patient does not fall through the cracks
